title: GABA-A receptors: how sedatives and benzodiazepines calm a neuron
ariaLabel: Schematic of a GABA-A receptor on a neuron: GABA released by inhibitory nerves opens a chloride channel, chloride enters, and the neuron fires less. Benzodiazepines make the channel open more often, barbiturates make it stay open longer, and flumazenil blocks the benzodiazepine effect.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or lipid value is shown or implied.
blockInfo: A drug of the chosen class acting at this step (generic teaching symbol, not a named drug's shape). Less passes here, with the effects shown at the cholesterol and the LDL receptors.

nodes.label: GABA
nodes.info: The main inhibitory transmitter of the brain, released by inhibitory nerve endings. The slider sets how much is released.

nodes.label: GABA-A chloride channel
nodes.info: GABA binds the GABA-A receptor and the chloride channel opens. Benzodiazepines bind a separate site and make opening more frequent; barbiturates make it last longer.

nodes.label: Chloride enters
nodes.info: Chloride flows into the neuron and makes it harder to fire.

nodes.label: Neuron firing
nodes.info: A teaching score for how readily the neuron fires. More chloride entry means less firing.

edges.label: GABA-A receptor
edges.info: The GABA-A receptor channel. Enhancers (benzodiazepines, barbiturates) increase the effect of a given amount of GABA, shown as a stronger flow. Flumazenil blocks the benzodiazepine site so the benzodiazepine effect goes.

sources: Where each class acts. Benzodiazepines increase how often GABA-A channels open, barbiturates increase how long they stay open, and flumazenil is a benzodiazepine-site antagonist. This is standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and were not checked against a linked source here, so they are flagged for review.
simplified: Z-drugs, alcohol, anaesthetics at GABA-A, direct channel opening by barbiturates at high levels, receptor subunits, tolerance and dependence, withdrawal, respiratory depression, flumazenil limits and adverse effects are left out. Neuron firing is drawn as a teaching score. Levels and the size of each effect are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
